title: The Deconstruction Course
summary: A close reading of Derrida's Plato's Pharmacy.
description: A study circle collectively reading Jacques Derrida's essay "Plato's Pharmacy" begins this Saturday (August 1st). Its aim, quite simply, is to offer an introduction to the French philosopher — or, more accurately, anti-philosopher — named Jacques Derrida.

We know that well-known introductions to Derrida have already been given in our country throughout the 1990s. Alongside Deepthi Kumara Gunaratne's Art and Deconstruction, and the articles he wrote on this subject in journals such as Pravada, Mathota, and London; Nalin Swaris's essay "Derrida's Deconstruction and the Buddha's Anatta-vada as Social Critique"; Rohan Perera's rather different essay "When Derrida Deconstructs Before an Asian Buddhist Woman"; one could also place the various writings of Desmond Mallikarachchi, Sasanka Perera, Saman Wickramaarachchi, K. K. Saman Kumara, Nalin de Silva, and others.

But what we are going to do is not add yet another introduction to this long list of “introductions to Derrida.” Instead, what we are going to do is something no one has done before: read Derrida collectively and closely. We are trying to reconstruct Derridean deconstruction in the Sinhala language. Put differently, we are not trying to offer summaries such as “for Derrida, difference is more primordial than identity…” Instead, we are trying to dissect one of Derrida's own sutra-like essays sentence by sentence. This will therefore create space for the experience of actually reading Derrida.

This is extremely challenging, because “reading” is something Derrida takes very seriously. The method we have used for years to render philosophers' ideas into Sinhala will be sharply tested here. This is precisely why this is, in no way, a “popular project.” It is a difficult exercise that takes time. But anyone interested in such a thing can take part in this. This does not require agreement with our political or philosophical positions. Anyone interested, for whatever reason, in gaining a high level of understanding of Derrida can take part in this. This is why we invite everyone who wishes to study this to join us.

K. K. Saman Kumara famously called Derridean deconstruction a “magic wand.” In our honest view, this description still holds, more or less, to this day. “Derrida” and “deconstruction” remain, for many in our country, a magic wand. If you want to know how this magic trick is done, come to the Mahaweli Centre in Colombo to join our Derrida reading, held every Saturday at 10:30 AM.

title: Postmodernism
summary: A close reading of Lyotard's work.
description: The aim of this course is to offer an introduction to postmodernism. For this, we closely read Jean-François Lyotard's work The Postmodern Condition. A written Sinhala introduction to each day's reading portion is provided. That text is composed with the aim of reconstructing Lyotard's work in the Sinhala language. It cannot be called a translation or an adaptation, because it includes additional clarifications and illustrations for the parts of Lyotard's ideas that are not so clear. But its real aim is that, by the end of reading that text, one gains an understanding of everything contained in Lyotard's work. In that sense, this can also be described as a kind of “translation.”

We are beginning this as part of a long-term project that opens up the philosophical foundations of a certain intellectual era we call “the 90s.” Accordingly, in addition to Lyotard, we will in future be offering similar introductions to the original works of thinkers such as Jacques Derrida and Michel Foucault. Rather than reading introductions written by others about them, our aim is to read the original works themselves. As we see it, a thinker truly confronts us only when we read his or her own original writing. What we have here is the first step in that direction. Through it, one gains the ability to understand the historical context of the new philosophical ideas we are proposing.

But taking part in this in no way requires becoming part of our broader philosophical project. Instead, this is open to anyone who is interested in learning about postmodernism. We honestly believe there is no other place in Sri Lanka where one can gain this level of understanding of this work. A major reason for this is that the number of people in our country who have read Lyotard's work from beginning to end is extremely limited. We do not believe that even that limited circle organizes something like this. This is why we honestly do not believe there is any other place in our country where one can gain this kind of understanding of the classic investigative work on the idea of “postmodernism.”

This is not something said for the sake of “marketing” — it is a regrettable truth about the intellectual decline of our country. The Colombo School of Philosophy is our own small contribution toward carrying this society forward, away from this regrettable fate.
